'''Steven M. Smith''' (born {{Circa}} 1960) is Emeritus Professor of Plant Genetics and Biochemistry at the [[University of Tasmania]] in Australia and Chief Investigator in the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Plant Success in Nature and Agriculture.

== Education and early life ==
Smith was born and raised in [[Luton]], England, United Kingdom. He attended Luton Grammar School and [[Luton Sixth Form College]] before becoming an Assistant Scientific Officer at [[Rothamsted Research|Rothamsted Experimental Station]] in Harpenden, Hertfordshire. Working at Rothamsted inspired him to embark on a career in plant sciences and he obtained university entrance qualifications through ‘day-release’ and evening classes at Luton College of Technology.

== Career ==
He was awarded first class honours in Biological Sciences from the [[University of Leicester]], then went to [[Indiana University Bloomington|Indiana University]] in the United States to study for a master's degree under the supervision of Carlos Miller, the discoverer of [[kinetin]]. Smith returned to the United Kingdom to study for a PhD under the supervision of Professor [[R. John Ellis|Reginald Ellis]] at the [[University of Warwick]] during which time he conducted some of his research at the [[Plant Breeding Institute]], in Cambridge. He was then awarded a Fellowship to carry out research at the [[Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation|Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO)]] Division of Plant Industry in [[Canberra]], Australia. After a short period at the [[John Innes Centre|John Innes Institute]] in [[Norwich]], he was appointed to a lectureship in the Botany Department at the [[University of Edinburgh]]. He spent 20 years in [[Edinburgh]] rising to become Head of the Institute of Molecular Plant Sciences. He served the [[Scottish Funding Council|Scottish Higher Education Funding Council]] as a Teaching Quality Assessor and was External Examiner at [[Ngee Ann Polytechnic]] in [[Singapore]]. Following the award of an [[Australian Research Council]] [[Federation Fellowship]] in 2004, Smith moved to the [[University of Western Australia]] and became Winthrop Professor of Plant Genomics. He was founding member of the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence in Plant Energy Biology in 2005, and was a Chief Investigator until 2014. He also established and was Director of the Centre of Excellence for Plant Metabolomics. In 2015 he was appointed Professor of Plant Genetics and Biochemistry in the School of Biological Sciences at the [[University of Tasmania]]. In 2013 and 2014 he was awarded Fellowships by the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]] and appointed Visiting Professor in the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology in [[Beijing]]. 

== Research ==
Smith's research is directed towards understanding plant growth and development at the molecular level, and seeking ways to improve plant productivity and value.

During his PhD studies Smith collaborated with John Bedbrook at the Plant Breeding Institute to clone the first [[Complementary DNA|cDNA]] encoding a plant enzyme.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Molecular cloning and sequencing of cDNA encoding the precursor to the small subunit of chloroplast ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase|journal = Nature|date = 1980-10-23|pages = 692–697|volume = 287|issue = 5784|doi = 10.1038/287692a0|first1 = John R.|last1 = Bedbrook|first2 = Steven M.|last2 = Smith|first3 = R. John|last3 = Ellis| bibcode=1980Natur.287..692B |s2cid = 4243808}}</ref> This enzyme is ribulose-1,5-''bis''phosphate carboxylase/oxygenase, abbreviated to [[RuBisCO]], which is responsible for carbon dioxide fixation by plants. In Edinburgh in the pre-genomics era, he collaborated with [[Chris J. Leaver|Chris Leaver]] and cloned several key enzymes of plant metabolism, including malate synthase, isocitrate lyase and PEP carboxykinase. He conceived an idea with [[Anthony Trewavas]] of creating transgenic plants expressing the calcium-sensitive luminous jellyfish protein, [[aequorin]], to report calcium signalling in plants. Together they obtained funding, created the plants and showed that they could report rapid calcium signalling in response to cold, fungi, touch and wind.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Transgenic plant aequorin reports the effects of touch and cold-shock and elicitors on cytoplasmic calcium|journal = Nature|date = 1991-08-08|pages = 524–526|volume = 352|issue = 6335|doi = 10.1038/352524a0|first1 = Marc R.|last1 = Knight|first2 = Anthony K.|last2 = Campbell|first3 = Steven M.|last3 = Smith|first4 = Anthony J.|last4 = Trewavas|pmid=1865907| bibcode=1991Natur.352..524K |s2cid = 4239898}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title = Wind-induced plant motion immediately increases cytosolic calcium|journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|date = 1992-06-01|issn = 0027-8424|pmc = 49209|pmid = 11536497|pages = 4967–4971|volume = 89|issue = 11|first1 = M. R.|last1 = Knight|first2 = S. M.|last2 = Smith|first3 = A. J.|last3 = Trewavas|doi=10.1073/pnas.89.11.4967| bibcode=1992PNAS...89.4967K |doi-access = free}}</ref> This work predated similar research using [[green fluorescent protein]] from the same jellyfish. In 1996, Smith and his PhD student Takeshi Takaha reported the discovery of cyclic glucans containing up to 200 glucose residues, which they named [[cycloamylose]].<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Potato D-enzyme Catalyzes the Cyclization of Amylose to Produce Cycloamylose, a Novel Cyclic Glucan|journal = Journal of Biological Chemistry|date = 1996-02-09|issn = 0021-9258|pages = 2902–2908|volume = 271|issue = 6|doi = 10.1074/jbc.271.6.2902|pmid = 8621678|first1 = Takeshi|last1 = Takaha|first2 = Michiyo|last2 = Yanase|first3 = Hiroki|last3 = Takata|first4 = Shigetaka|last4 = Okada|first5 = Steven M.|last5 = Smith|doi-access = free}}</ref> Cycloamylose and related cycloglucans are now used extensively in food and biotechnology industries. Further research on starch metabolism with Alison Smith and Sam Zeeman at the John Innes Centre led to the discovery of a novel pathway of starch breakdown in leaves.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Starch Degradation|journal = Annual Review of Plant Biology|date = 2005-01-01|pmid = 15862090|pages = 73–98|volume = 56|issue = 1|doi = 10.1146/annurev.arplant.56.032604.144257|first1 = Alison M.|last1 = Smith|first2 = Samuel C.|last2 = Zeeman|first3 = Steven M.|last3 = Smith}}</ref> Smith was also instrumental in defining pathways of energy metabolism involving peroxisomes, particularly fatty acid [[Beta oxidation|beta-oxidation]] and the [[glyoxylate cycle]].<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Arabidopsis Peroxisomal Citrate Synthase Is Required for Fatty Acid Respiration and Seed Germination|journal = The Plant Cell|date = 2005-07-01|issn = 1532-298X|pmc = 1167550|pmid = 15923350|pages = 2037–2048|volume = 17|issue = 7|doi = 10.1105/tpc.105.031856|first1 = Itsara|last1 = Pracharoenwattana|first2 = Johanna E.|last2 = Cornah|first3 = Steven M.|last3 = Smith}}</ref>

== Karrikins: a new family of plant growth regulators ==
Smith's current and most important contribution to plant biology lies in the establishment of [[karrikin]]s as a major family of naturally occurring plant growth regulators, determination of karrikin mode of action and evolution of the karrikin response.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = What are karrikins and how were they 'discovered' by plants?|journal = BMC Biology|date = 2015-12-21|pmc = 4687367|pmid = 26689715|volume = 13|issue = 1|pages = 108|doi = 10.1186/s12915-015-0219-0|language = En|first1 = Gavin R.|last1 = Flematti|first2 = Kingsley W|last2 = Dixon|first3 = Steven M.|last3 = Smith | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title = Smoke linked to stronger, thicker plant growth|url = https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2010-mar-30-la-sci-smoke30-2010mar30-story.html|newspaper = Los Angeles Times|date = 2010-03-30|access-date = 2015-09-03|issn = 0458-3035|first = Amina|last = Khan}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title = Finding the signalling system for plant 'smoke' response|url = http://www.sciencewa.net.au/topics/environment-a-conservation/item/2993-finding-the-signalling-system-for-plant-smoke-response/2993-finding-the-signalling-system-for-plant-smoke-response|access-date = 2015-09-03|first = Geoff|last = Vivian}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title = Groundbreaking plant scientist joined the University of Tasmania|url = http://www.weeklytimesnow.com.au/agribusiness/cropping/groundbreaking-plant-scientist-joined-the-university-of-tasmania/story-fnker6ee-1227144288889|access-date = 2015-09-03|date = 2014-12-04}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title = Bushfire science helping seeds germinate quicker and stronger|url = http://www.abc.net.au/news/2014-06-30/bushfire-germination-rice-crops/5559446|website = ABC Rural|access-date = 2015-09-03|date = 2014-06-30}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title = Chemicals in smoke can help forests regenerate after fire {{!}} Pacific Beat|url = http://www.radioaustralia.net.au/international/radio/onairhighlights/chemicals-in-smoke-can-help-forests-regenerate-after-fire|website = www.radioaustralia.net.au|access-date = 2015-09-03}}</ref> Karrikins are small organic compounds produced by [[Bushfires in Australia|bushfires]]. They are washed into the soil by rain and stimulate germination of dormant seeds of fire-following plants that reside in the soil seed-bank.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Karrikins Discovered in Smoke Trigger Arabidopsis Seed Germination by a Mechanism Requiring Gibberellic Acid Synthesis and Light|journal = Plant Physiology|date = 2009-02-01|issn = 1532-2548|pmc = 2633839|pmid = 19074625|pages = 863–873|volume = 149|issue = 2|doi = 10.1104/pp.108.131516|first1 = David C.|last1 = Nelson|first2 = Julie-Anne|last2 = Riseborough|first3 = Gavin R.|last3 = Flematti|first4 = Jason|last4 = Stevens|first5 = Emilio L.|last5 = Ghisalberti|first6 = Kingsley W.|last6 = Dixon|first7 = Steven M.|last7 = Smith}}</ref> This response to karrikins is a specific evolutionary adaption of numerous fire-following plant species, providing them with the opportunity to grow and reproduce successfully in the post-fire environment.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Karrikins enhance light responses during germination and seedling development in Arabidopsis thaliana|journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|date = 2010-04-13|issn = 0027-8424|pmc = 2872431|pmid = 20351290|pages = 7095–7100|volume = 107|issue = 15|doi = 10.1073/pnas.0911635107|first1 = David C.|last1 = Nelson|first2 = Gavin R.|last2 = Flematti|first3 = Julie-Anne|last3 = Riseborough|first4 = Emilio L.|last4 = Ghisalberti|first5 = Kingsley W.|last5 = Dixon|first6 = Steven M.|last6 = Smith| bibcode=2010PNAS..107.7095N |doi-access = free}}</ref>

Smith discovered that ''[[Arabidopsis thaliana]]'' can respond to karrikins under specific conditions and this provided the breakthrough required to discover their mode of action.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = F-box protein MAX2 has dual roles in karrikin and strigolactone signaling in Arabidopsis thaliana|journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|date = 2011-05-24|issn = 0027-8424|pmc = 3102411|pmid = 21555559|pages = 8897–8902|volume = 108|issue = 21|doi = 10.1073/pnas.1100987108|first1 = David C.|last1 = Nelson|first2 = Adrian|last2 = Scaffidi|first3 = Elizabeth == Personal ==
Smith is married to Dr. Brenda Winning and they have one daughter, born in 1998.
Smith is a side drummer in the City of Hobart Highland Pipe Band.
